title: ‘Why can’t a student who critically analyses football, not do the same for a text in the classroom?’ or transferable skills in the classroom -not-do-the-same-for-a-text-in-the-classroom-or-transferable-skills-in-the-classroom/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino uses a Year 11 footballer who is disciplined on the pitch but disorganised in lessons to question the idea that skills transfer readily between domains. She argues that organisation, communication and critical thinking cannot be transferred without a secure base of knowledge in the new domain. Relating every lesson to student interests is not the answer, since the curriculum cannot be built from tenuous links. Instead she lists the ingredients of a knowledge base: explicit instruction, modelling, checks for understanding, practice, and review and retrieval. She acknowledges that behaviour management and early success are needed so that students like Alex can engage at all. The conclusion is that skills must be rebuilt through knowledge in each new domain rather than assumed to carry over.
points: Skills such as goal-setting and critical analysis do not automatically transfer between domains, as the footballer-in-the-classroom example shows.
Secure domain knowledge is the precondition for applying a skill, and being surrounded by something does not build knowledge.
Making all content relate to individual student interests is neither feasible nor the point of a curriculum.
Explicit instruction, modelling, checks for understanding, practice and retrieval form the recipe for a strong knowledge base.
Consistent behaviour management plus early successes can counter students' belief that they cannot achieve in a subject.
quotes: Over the years, I have had a number of students similar to Alex. They show excellent skills in one domain but cannot seem to transfer them to another.

One might say that Alex is not engaged in my classroom and that I should relate my subject to his interests to motivate him. But this does not work unless the point of our curriculum is to make tenuous links to student interests.

All of the skills I have mentioned already (and many more) are important. We want our students to communicate well, set themselves achievable goals, know how to work in a team or lead when necessary. But none of these things are transferable without knowledge at their heart.
At home, all I ever hear about is football but I only know enough to repeat what I hear without any thought. I certainly cannot critically analyse a match no matter how many times I watch it.

just because someone is nodding along to what you say, doesn’t mean they understand it. Check that they don’t hold misconceptions (like me with the offside rule!) or are making the wrong meaning from your explanation, or think they know how to do something but actually haven’t automated the steps.

Here, the answer is a combination of consistent behaviour management and providing chances of success so they can see that they can achieve in this subject. I use homework together with a lot of work in the classroom to build success and confidence in my students.
